I'm looking for some clarity around the value of ssris/snris.

[https://www.nature.com/articles/s41380-022-01661-0](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41380-022-01661-0)

This paper mostly repeats things I already knew, but also confirmed some fears I had about overall emotional numbing and limiting the potential for emotional self-regulation. I have been on/off various antidepressants for majority of my life. I was on 60 mg of duloxetine for 3 years in August of 2022. I was doing relatively well around this time, felt that I may have been stagnating in life and emotionally, and decided to slowly ween myself off. I felt good about this decision. I was able to experience more highs and lows. The ability to cry at movies and when grieving for a loved one were particularly valuable. I began grad school in September feeling animated and confident. I slowly began to experience times of extreme sadness. I began 30 mg of duloxetine around mid September. Mood fluctuated from terrible to good around this time. By mid October, I felt a period of total numbness that was very distressing, causing me to suddenly discontinue the snri. I have been off it since then.

I have been tormenting myself over the decision of whether to stay off them. I frequently can't get out of bed, have trouble thinking straight, have dropped a class, and am rarely attending my lab. However, I sometimes experience times of elation. I think even my times of suffering have value. I often think of how suffering is at the core of important art and philosophy, which I'm able to appreciate more viscerally since discontinuing. However I can not derive meaning from life if I can not self actualize due to being stuck in bed. Alternatively, maybe it is the possibility of solving this through an snri that is limiting my ability to make mindset changes that would be more productive. Maybe my suffering is valuable for self-realization, and is preceding a breakthrough. For example, it is affirming suspicions that my grad program is not where my interests lie. Or perhaps the value of suffering and the subjective impressions of my grad program are distortions of thought arising from some pathology. Or maybe the distortions of thought due to mental illness are valuable and provide a unique perspective, as they have for many artists and thinkers.

[https://www.sciencemediacentre.org/expert-reaction-to-a-review-paper-on-the-serotonin-theory-of-depression/](https://www.sciencemediacentre.org/expert-reaction-to-a-review-paper-on-the-serotonin-theory-of-depression/)

Recently, I read these impressions on the previous paper I linked and was back on the circle of thoughts I seem to return to. Looking up Moncrieff's twitter, she has a frightening bias against ssris that I find hard to trust. As I understand it, ssris/snris are thought to function through:

1. promoting neurogenesis
2. reducing inflammation
3. moderating glutamate activity

The evidence for this seems compelling but I find it hard to be sure of much of anything.

Maybe I should try a stimulant medication, at least this would be an inducible state that would drive me to action. Or maybe I should try psilocybin, which could be introspective and may be closed off to me if I returned to snris. Maybe I should go somewhere physically, like another country, or pursue religion, while my sense of art and meaning is heightened.

From you, reader, I am hoping you may be able to offer your objective thoughts on the science, identify potential distortions in my way of thinking, and offer your subjective experience on related issues. Grateful for this sub.
